questions.question: What is the primary value of an AI champion?
options: Becoming the single approver so every AI use case passes through one consistent reviewer
Turning scattered experiments into reusable assets, shared standards, and better team habits
Taking over the governance team's mandate for policy, compliance sign-off, and risk decisions
Keeping the team's best prompts in a private library so quality stays under one person's control
questions.explanation: Champions scale learning and reuse without becoming the only decision point. The lesson is explicit that a champion helps the team reuse what works rather than owning every AI decision.

questions.question: Three people ask the same prompt question in meetings this month. What does the enablement loop do with that?
options: It is answered individually each time, keeping the champion close to the team's daily work
It is escalated to governance, since repeated confusion signals a policy gap to be closed
It is logged as a training request and passed to the vendor's own enablement programme
It becomes a backlog item, so the answer is built once as a reviewed, shareable asset
questions.explanation: The enablement loop starts at recurring questions and turns them into backlog items, so learning becomes a reusable asset instead of staying local and fragile. Escalation is reserved for risks, not for repetition.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A certificate engine that issues completion badges to session attendees
A fine-tuned model trained on the team's collected prompts and answers
A cloud deployment of the shared prompt library as an internal service
A ranked champion backlog with priority, controls, and rationale
questions.explanation: The artifact prioritizes champion activities - office hours, reusable assets, brown bags, and escalation support - and returns priority, controls, and rationale for each.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: An office hours plan that gives the team a regular, predictable slot to bring questions
An open channel where every request is answered ad hoc, whenever it happens to arrive
A rule that shared assets are published immediately, so review does not slow reuse down
A standing agreement that the champion absorbs risky questions instead of passing them on
questions.explanation: Office hours are one practical champion enablement control. The backlog and the quality rubric exist so enablement does not decay into random support work or unreviewed publishing.

questions.question: When should champion work escalate rather than stay as informal support?
options: When impact, uncertainty, or risk signals are high enough to need the right owner
When the same question has already been answered in a previous office hours session
When the request comes from outside the champion's own team and department
When the reusable asset has not yet passed its quality review with the community
questions.explanation: Champions should escalate high-risk or unclear issues to the right owners rather than silently absorbing them.

questions.question: Why does the course use a champion backlog?
options: To focus enablement on repeated team needs and turn them into reusable assets
To keep incoming requests out of the community channel so the queue stays short
To let assets be shared before quality review, since speed matters more than polish
To replace office hours with a written queue that the champion works through alone
questions.explanation: The backlog keeps champion work focused and reusable, which prevents enablement from becoming random support work.
